claims.text: High aggregate accuracy hides 30-43% of errors in a rare Type 4-2 verb subtype.
claims.poster_quote: High aggregate accuracy hides 30-43% of errors in a rare Type 4-2 verb subtype.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: a single structurally specific irregular subtype, verbs whose stems end in /e/ and require gemination before the past-tense suffix and make up fewer than 1% of the data, accounts for a disproportionate 30–43% share of residual errors
claims.reason: Section 6.4, Table 4, and Figure 1 confirm that Type 4-2 verbs, which are 0.9% of the data, account for 30-43% of residual errors.

claims.text: Removing Type 4-2 boosts accuracy more than removing all irregulars.
claims.poster_quote: Removing it boosts accuracy more than removing all irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain: 97.73% → 99.75% (+2.02), corresponding to an approximately 89% reduction in error rate. The gain is substantially larger than removing all irregular verbs (+1.22).
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 6 show that removing Type 4-2 alone results in the largest accuracy gain for LST and PGT compared to removing all irregular verbs.

claims.text: Gemination-related errors dominate residual failures.
claims.poster_quote: Gemination-related errors dominate residual failures.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors (omission and insertion combined) dominate residual failures, accounting for 75.5% (PGT) and 80.3% (LST) of all errors.
claims.reason: Section 6.3 and Table 3 confirm that gemination-related errors are the most frequent type of residual failure in both models.

claims.text: Type 4-2 contributes 34-48× its proportional share to total errors.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 contributes 34-48× its proportional share to total errors.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 contributes 34–48× its proportional representation to total errors, as visualized in Figure 2, the largest disparity of any subclass in either system.
claims.reason: Section 6.4 and Table 5 confirm that Type 4-2 contributes 34–48× its proportional share to total errors.

claims.text: Error concentration stems from low-frequency patterns interacting with orthography.
claims.poster_quote: Error concentration stems from low-frequency patterns interacting with orthography.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: error concentration in neural morphological learning is not driven by irregularity per se, but by the interaction between extreme low-frequency morphological patterns and specific orthographic processes.
claims.reason: The abstract and Section 7 explicitly state that error concentration is due to the interaction between low-frequency patterns and orthography.

claims.text: Both models hit ~97% accuracy.
claims.poster_quote: Both models hit ~97% accuracy.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: On the primary run, both systems achieve high aggregate accuracy on the full dataset: 97.98% (PGT) and 97.73% (LST).
claims.reason: Section 6.1 confirms that both models achieve approximately 97% accuracy.

claims.text: Type 4-2 verbs cause 30-43% of errors despite being 0.9% of data.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 verbs cause 30-43% of errors despite being 0.9% of data.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 verbs are massively overrepresented, accounting for 30.2% (PGT) and 43.1% (LST) of all errors while comprising just 0.9% of the dataset.
claims.reason: Section 6.4 and Table 4 confirm that Type 4-2 verbs cause 30-43% of errors despite being 0.9% of the data.

claims.text: Gemination errors dominate.
claims.poster_quote: Gemination errors dominate.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Gemination-related errors (omission and insertion combined) dominate residual failures, accounting for 75.5% (PGT) and 80.3% (LST) of all errors.
claims.reason: Section 6.3 and Table 3 confirm that gemination errors dominate residual failures.

claims.text: Aggregate scores mask structural failure.
claims.poster_quote: Aggregate scores mask structural failure.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: high aggregate accuracy is a stable property of both architectures. Despite this overall stability, errors cluster in specific low-frequency subclasses.
claims.reason: Section 6.1 and 6.4 discuss how high aggregate accuracy masks structural failures in low-frequency subclasses.

claims.text: Use Disparity Ratio to evaluate subclasses.
claims.poster_quote: Use Disparity Ratio to evaluate subclasses.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Per-item predictions can be regrouped by structural subclass and scored with the Disparity Ratio metric introduced in §5.4.
claims.reason: Section 7 explicitly recommends using the Disparity Ratio to evaluate subclasses.

claims.text: Not all irregularity harms generalization — only specific low-frequency patterns.
claims.poster_quote: Not all irregularity harms generalization — only specific low-frequency patterns.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Irregularity is not uniformly detrimental to neural morphological learning. A single low-frequency subtype, verbs requiring gemination after a stem-final /e/, is structurally distinct from other irregulars.
claims.reason: Section 7 explicitly states that not all irregularity harms generalization, but specific low-frequency patterns do.

claims.text: Type 4-2 error rate is 43% for PGT.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 error rate: 43% (PGT)
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 shows an error rate of 43% (PGT).
claims.reason: Figure 1 confirms that the Type 4-2 error rate is 43% for PGT.

claims.text: Type 4-2 error rate is 60% for LST.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 error rate: 60% (LST)
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 shows an error rate of 43% (PGT) and 60% (LST).
claims.reason: Figure 1 confirms that the Type 4-2 error rate is 60% for LST.

claims.text: Disparity Ratio is 34-48× its data share.
claims.poster_quote: Disparity Ratio: 34-48× its data share
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 contributes 34–48× its proportional representation to total errors, as visualized in Figure 2, the largest disparity of any subclass in either system.
claims.reason: Section 6.4 and Table 5 confirm the Disparity Ratio for Type 4-2 is 34-48× its data share.

claims.text: Errors are stable across seeds and architectures.
claims.poster_quote: Errors stable across seeds and architectures
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: This consistency, together with the seed-level stability reported in §6.1, suggests the failures reflect systematic properties of orthographic representation rather than idiosyncrasies of a single model.
claims.reason: Section 6.5 confirms that errors are stable across seeds and architectures.

claims.text: Evaluation should subgroup by morphology.
claims.poster_quote: Evaluation should subgroup by morphology
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Evaluation protocols for data-efficient pretraining may therefore benefit from subgroup-aware diagnostics of the kind proposed here, and not aggregate accuracy alone.
claims.reason: Section 7 explicitly recommends subgrouping by morphology for evaluation.

claims.text: Type 4-2 sensitivity may persist in LLMs.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 sensitivity may persist in LLMs
claims.label: unsupported
claims.reason: The paper does not provide evidence or explicitly state that Type 4-2 sensitivity may persist in large language models (LLMs).

claims.text: Metric generalizes to other morphologically rich languages.
claims.poster_quote: Metric generalizes to other morphologically rich languages
claims.label: unsupported
claims.reason: The paper does not provide evidence or explicitly state that the metric generalizes to other morphologically rich languages.

claims.text: Hiragana-only Japanese verb data is used, excluding canonical irregulars.
claims.poster_quote: We use hiragana-only Japanese verb data, excluding canonical irregulars.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: All forms are converted to hiragana to maintain orthographic consistency and eliminate confounds introduced by kanji homography.
claims.reason: Section 3 confirms that the dataset uses hiragana-only Japanese verb data and excludes canonical irregulars.

claims.text: Type 4-2 verbs are 0.9% of data but structurally distinct.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 verbs are 0.9% of data but structurally distinct.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 is the smallest structurally coherent subclass, comprising only 0.9% of the data.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 and Table 1 confirm that Type 4-2 verbs are 0.9% of the data and are structurally distinct.

claims.text: The dataset includes Type 4-1 (119 verbs, stem-final /i/ + gemination).
claims.poster_quote: The dataset includes Type 4-1 (119 verbs, stem-final /i/ + gemination)
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-1: stem-final /i/ + gemination, e.g. まじる majiru → まじった majitta. Count: 119.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 confirms the dataset includes Type 4-1 with 119 verbs.

claims.text: The dataset includes Type 4-3 (1 verb, ��→���).
claims.poster_quote: The dataset includes Type 4-3 (1 verb, ��→���)
claims.label: supported

claims.reason: Section 3.1 confirms the dataset includes Type 4-3 with 1 verb.

claims.text: Type 4-2 is the smallest coherent subclass.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2 being the smallest coherent subclass.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2 is the smallest structurally coherent subclass, comprising only 0.9% of the data.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 confirms that Type 4-2 is the smallest coherent subclass.

claims.text: All forms are converted to hiragana to eliminate kanji homography confounds.
claims.poster_quote: All forms are converted to hiragana to eliminate kanji homography confounds.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: All forms are converted to hiragana to maintain orthographic consistency and eliminate confounds introduced by kanji homography.
claims.reason: Section 3 confirms that all forms are converted to hiragana to eliminate kanji homography confounds.

claims.text: Type 1 includes 2,503 Godan verbs.
claims.poster_quote: Type 1: 2,503 Godan verbs
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 1 (Godan): regular u-verbs, e.g. かく kaku → かいた kaita. Count: 2,503.

claims.text: Type 2 includes 1,298 Ichidan verbs.
claims.poster_quote: Type 2: 1,298 Ichidan verbs
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 2 (Ichidan): regular ru-verbs, e.g. たべる taberu → たべた tabeta. Count: 1,298.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 and Table 1 confirm that Type 2 includes 1,298 Ichidan verbs.

claims.text: Type 4-2 includes 37 verbs requiring /e/ + gemination.
claims.poster_quote: Type 4-2: 37 verbs requiring /e/ + gemination
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Type 4-2: stem-final /e/ + gemination, e.g. あきれかえる akirekaeru → あきれかえった akirekaetta. Count: 37.
claims.reason: Section 3.1 and Table 1 confirm that Type 4-2 includes 37 verbs requiring /e/ + gemination.

claims.text: Removing only Type 4-2 boosts accuracy most: +2.02% for LST.
claims.poster_quote: Removing only Type 4-2 boosts accuracy most: +2.02% (LST)
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain: 97.73% → 99.75% (+2.02), corresponding to an approximately 89% reduction in error rate.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 6 confirm that removing only Type 4-2 boosts accuracy most for LST (+2.02%).

claims.text: Removing only Type 4-2 boosts accuracy most: +1.00% for PGT.
claims.poster_quote: Removing only Type 4-2 boosts accuracy most: +1.00% (PGT)
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the PGT system, removing Type 4-2 alone is still the single best condition (97.98% → 98.98%, +1.00).
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 6 confirm that removing only Type 4-2 boosts accuracy most for PGT (+1.00%).

claims.text: Irregularity alone isn’t the problem — structure is.
claims.poster_quote: Irregularity alone isn’t the problem — structure is.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: error concentration in neural morphological learning is not driven by irregularity per se, but by the interaction between extreme low-frequency morphological patterns and specific orthographic processes.
claims.reason: The abstract and Section 7 explicitly state that irregularity alone isn’t the problem, but structure is.

claims.text: PGT uses pointer-generator copying with input attention.
claims.poster_quote: PGT uses pointer-generator copying with input attention
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The first is a Pointer-Generator Transformer (henceforth PGT), incorporating a pointer-generator copying mechanism (See et al., 2017) with attention over the input lemma.
claims.reason: Section 4 confirms that PGT uses a pointer-generator copying mechanism with input attention.

claims.text: LST uses lemma-split regime to improve generalization.
claims.poster_quote: LST uses lemma-split regime to improve generalization
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: The second follows the architecture of Goldman et al. (2023), a Lemma-Split Transformer (henceforth LST) that additionally uses a lemma-split training and evaluation regime, preventing a lemma from appearing in both training and test data and improving generalization to unseen lemmas.
claims.reason: Section 4 confirms that LST uses a lemma-split regime to improve generalization.

claims.text: Both models use cross-entropy loss, teacher forcing, Adam, and standard Transformer scheduling.
claims.poster_quote: Both use cross-entropy loss, teacher forcing, Adam, and standard Transformer scheduling.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Both models are trained with cross-entropy loss and teacher forcing, using the default hyperparameter configurations from their respective shared-task baselines (Vylomova et al., 2020; Goldman et al., 2023), optimized with Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) and standard Transformer learning-rate scheduling (Vaswani et al., 2017).
claims.reason: Section 5.1 confirms that both models use cross-entropy loss, teacher forcing, Adam, and standard Transformer scheduling.

claims.text: Error taxonomy includes 6 orthography-sensitive failure modes.
claims.poster_quote: Error taxonomy includes 6 orthography-sensitive failure modes.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: We defined a taxonomy of six orthography- and morphophonology-sensitive failure modes (Table 2): gemination omission, gemination insertion, phonological substitution, morpheme boundary errors, character recognition (UNK) errors, and compound verb structural errors.
claims.reason: Section 6.2 and Table 2 confirm that the error taxonomy includes six orthography-sensitive failure modes.

claims.text: LST achieves 99.75% accuracy after removing Type 4-2.
claims.poster_quote: LST: 99.75% accuracy after -4-2
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 yields the largest observed gain: 97.73% → 99.75% (+2.02).
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 7 confirm that LST achieves 99.75% accuracy after removing Type 4-2.

claims.text: PGT’s best single ablation is still removing Type 4-2.
claims.poster_quote: PGT: best single ablation is still -4-2
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: For the PGT system, removing Type 4-2 alone is still the single best condition (97.98% → 98.98%, +1.00).
claims.reason: Section 6.7 and Table 7 confirm that PGT’s best single ablation is still removing Type 4-2.

claims.text: Retaining Type 4-1/4-3 costs little — structure matters.
claims.poster_quote: Retaining 4-1/4-3 costs little — structure matters
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Some irregular subtypes (4-1, 4-3) can be retained without cost: in the LST system, removing only Type 4-2 while retaining 4-1 and 4-3 (condition −4-2) achieves 99.75%.
claims.reason: Section 6.7 confirms that retaining Type 4-1/4-3 costs little and that structure matters.

claims.text: Single-run ablations were performed.
claims.poster_quote: Single-run ablations; single language, paradigm, and architectures.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Our ablation experiments were each run once per condition; replication across multiple training runs would strengthen the causal claim.
claims.reason: The Limitations section explicitly states that single-run ablations were performed.

claims.text: Single language, paradigm, and architectures were used.
claims.poster_quote: Single-run ablations; single language, paradigm, and architectures.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: our study focuses on a single language, a single morphological paradigm, and two Transformer-based architectures.
claims.reason: The Limitations section confirms that a single language, paradigm, and architectures were used.

claims.text: No sensitive data was used.
claims.poster_quote: No sensitive data.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: This work involves no sensitive data, human subjects, or personally identifiable information.
claims.reason: The Ethics Statement confirms that no sensitive data was used.

claims.text: Future work includes cross-linguistic, frequency-matched, IPA/romanization tests.
claims.poster_quote: Future work: cross-linguistic, frequency-matched, IPA/romanization tests.
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Future Directions. The structural confusability effect identified here raises two natural extensions. First, whether the same effect appears when models are evaluated zero-shot at scale, testing whether frontier language models show the same Type 4-2 sensitivity or whether scale eliminates the inductive bias. Second, whether the Disparity Ratio metric generalizes beyond Japanese to other morphologically rich languages, testing whether structural confusability constitutes a domain-general constraint on morphological learning.
claims.reason: Section 'Future Directions' explicitly mentions cross-linguistic validation and evaluation under alternative input representations (e.g., IPA or romanization).

claims.text: Replication across seeds is needed.
claims.poster_quote: Replication across seeds needed
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Limitations. First, our ablation experiments were each run once per condition; replication across multiple training runs would strengthen the causal claim.
claims.reason: The 'Limitations' section explicitly states that replication across multiple training runs is needed to strengthen the causal claim.

claims.text: Test scale: do LLMs overcome this bias?
claims.poster_quote: Test scale: do LLMs overcome this bias?
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Future Directions. First, whether the same effect appears when models are evaluated zero-shot at scale, testing whether frontier language models show the same Type 4-2 sensitivity or whether scale eliminates the inductive bias.
claims.reason: The 'Future Directions' section explicitly proposes testing whether large language models overcome the identified bias.

claims.text: Mechanism: frequency vs. structure interaction?
claims.poster_quote: Mechanism: frequency vs. structure interaction?
claims.label: supported
claims.paper_evidence: Limitations. Our analysis is correlational with respect to the specific mechanism (frequency vs. structural complexity vs. their interaction) underlying Type 4-2’s distinctiveness; the ablation results support a causal role for this subtype’s presence in training data, but do not isolate frequency from structural complexity as independent factors.
claims.reason: The 'Limitations' section explicitly discusses the need to isolate frequency and structural complexity as independent factors.
